title: Openings & Counters
blurb: Sound systems for both colors, and how to punish early mistakes.

items.title: The three opening promises
items.sub: Center, development, king safety — every good opening keeps all three.
items.intro: Before memorizing lines, internalize the three promises every opening must keep: fight for the center, develop pieces quickly (knights before bishops, don't move the same piece twice), and castle early. Watch a model opening keep all three.
items.outro: Checklist for your next ten games: a center pawn on move one, knights and bishops out by move six, castled by move eight, no early queen adventures, no piece moved twice without a concrete reason.

steps.note: The pawn stakes a claim in the center and controls d5 and f5. It also frees the bishop and queen. Promise one — the center — is underway.
Black answers symmetrically, claiming an equal share of the center. Openings are a negotiation over these four central squares.
Development with a threat: the knight attacks e5. Moves that develop AND threaten something are the gold standard — your opponent must spend time responding.
Black defends e5 while developing. Notice neither side has touched a piece twice, or brought the queen out early.
The bishop takes its best diagonal, eyeing f7 — the weakest square on the board, defended only by the king. Now White is one move from castling.
Black mirrors, aiming at f2. Both sides have kept all three promises so far.
A small pawn move with a big idea: preparing d4 to build a full pawn center. Pawn moves in the opening are fine when they serve the center.
Black develops the last minor piece needed for castling and counter-attacks e4. Development with a threat, again.
White calmly defends e4. Not every move can be a threat — solid moves that hold your position together are just as valuable.
Black solidifies e5 and opens the light-squared bishop's diagonal.
Promise three, delivered: the king tucks into safety and the rook joins the game. Castling by move 6–8 should be your habit in almost every game.
Both kings are safe, all minor pieces developed, the center contested. This is what a healthy opening looks like — regardless of which named opening you play.

items.title: The Italian Game (as White)
items.sub: A complete, low-theory system after 1.e4 e5.
items.intro: The Italian is the ideal first opening for White: natural developing moves, a clear middlegame plan, and very little memorization. The modern treatment — the "quiet" Giuoco Pianissimo — aims for a slow buildup rather than early fireworks.
items.outro: Your plan from here, in order: 1) Nbd2, 2) re-route that knight to f1 and g3, 3) h3 already played — so look for the d4 break when your pieces all support it. If Black does nothing, expand with d4 and enjoy more space.

steps.note: Claim the center.
Black claims their share.
Attack e5 while developing.
Defended.

The defining move. The bishop points at f7. One caution as either color here: if Black plays an early ...Nf6 and White knows the Fried Liver Attack (Ng5!), things get sharp — as Black, prefer 3...Bc5 first.
The main, solid reply.
Preparing a slow d4 push, and giving the bishop a retreat on c2 via b3–c2 ideas later. c3 is the backbone of the whole system.
Black hits e4.
"Pianissimo" — very quiet. White builds a modest but rock-solid center and postpones the d4 break until fully developed.
Black matches the structure.
King safety, never postponed.
A useful little move: gives the c5-bishop a retreat on a7 and prepares ...b5 to gain queenside space.
White replies in kind, stopping ...b5 and grabbing space. These small pawn moves on the edge decide who gets free expansion later.
The bishop tucks away, safe from being traded, still staring at f2.
The rook supports e4. White's dream setup: Nbd2–f1–g3, h3, then finally d4 with everything protected.
Both sides castled.
Denying Black's bishop the g4 pin. Position complete: White will maneuver Nb1–d2–f1–g3 and prepare d4. You can reach this exact setup in game after game.

items.title: The Ruy Lopez, demystified
items.sub: The classical main line — and the logic behind every move.
items.intro: The Ruy Lopez (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5) looks scary because grandmasters play it 30 moves deep. But the first nine moves follow one simple thread: White pressures e5, Black keeps rescuing it, and both sides improve their pieces while arguing about it.
items.outro: The thread to remember: pressure the defender, keep improving, prepare d4. When your opponents play the Ruy against you as Black, follow the same recipe you just watched: a6, Nf6, Be7, b5, d6, O-O.

steps.note: Attacking e5.
Defending it.
The Spanish bishop attacks the DEFENDER of e5. Indirect pressure: White isn't threatening to win e5 yet (Bxc6 then Nxe5 lets Black regain the pawn with Qd4!), but the pressure shapes the whole game.
The classic question: capture or retreat? Putting the question to the bishop gains Black a useful tempo option later (...b5).
Retreating but keeping the pin-like pressure on c6.
Development plus a real threat on e4.
Bold: White ignores the threat! If 5...Nxe4, White plays 6.d4! and regains the pawn with a strong initiative while Black's knight dangles. Castling is also development.
Black declines the pawn grab and calmly prepares to castle. Wise — grabbing pawns before castling is how beginners lose miniatures.
Now e4 is genuinely defended, so White threatens Bxc6 followed by Nxe5 for real. Black must react.
Breaking the pressure on c6 once and for all by hitting the bishop.
The bishop lands on the same diagonal as the Italian — aiming at f7. Different route, same dream.
Reinforcing e5 and freeing the c8-bishop.
Two ideas: preparing the d4 center break, and giving the bishop an escape on c2 when Black plays ...Na5.
Preventing ...Bg4, which would pin the knight that supports the coming d4. This is the main-line position of the entire Ruy Lopez. Everything both sides did was about one square: e5.

items.title: The Queen's Gambit (as White)
items.sub: 1.d4 chess: pressure on d5 and the famous "gambit" that isn't.
items.intro: After 1.d4 d5 2.c4 White offers a pawn — but it's not really a gambit: if Black grabs c4, White regains it comfortably. The real idea is to pressure d5 and pull Black's center apart. This is the Queen's Gambit Declined main line, the most classical opening in chess.
items.outro: Remember the shape of the argument: c4 pressures d5, Bg5 undermines its defender, Rc1 pre-loads the c-file. If you play 1.d4, this one structure will appear in half your games.

steps.note: Like 1.e4, this stakes the center — but the d-pawn arrives already defended by the queen, so play tends to be slower and more strategic.
The gambit. White attacks d5 with a wing pawn, hoping to trade it off and dominate the center. If 2...dxc4, White plays e3 or e4 and picks the pawn back up — Black cannot hold it.
Declining. Black reinforces d5 sturdily. The cost: the c8-bishop is temporarily locked in. Much of Black's game will be about freeing it.
More pressure on d5.
More defense of d5. Count the battle: two attackers, two defenders.
Cunning: the bishop pins the knight to the queen, which UNDERMINES a defender of d5 without adding an attacker. Attacking a defender counts as attacking the target.
Breaking the pin. A pinned defender is an unreliable defender, so Black fixes it immediately.
Modest but necessary — opening the f1-bishop so White can castle.
A key idea: the knight supports its brother on f6 and prepares the freeing breaks ...dxc4 and ...c5 or ...e5. Cramped positions are fine IF you know your freeing moves.
The rook takes the file that will open when pawns trade on c4/d5. Placing rooks on soon-to-open files before they open is a master habit worth stealing.
Solid, supporting d5 again — the famous "triangle" structure c6+d5+e6.
The last minor piece develops, aiming at h7.
NOW Black captures — precisely when it costs the d3-bishop a second move to recapture. Timing a capture to cost the opponent a tempo: that's the level of "why" hidden in openings.
White happily recaptures with a fine game: more space and freer pieces. Black will follow with ...b5, ...Bb7 or the ...c5 break to fight back.

items.title: The London System (easy mode)
items.sub: One setup against nearly everything Black does.
items.intro: The London is beloved by club players because it's a SETUP, not a tree of variations: the same seven moves in almost any order, against almost anything. Perfect when you'd rather spend your study time on tactics and endgames.
items.outro: The London recipe: d4, Bf4, e3, c3, Nbd2, Ngf3, Bd3, O-O — then aim a knight at e5 and consider h4-ideas if Black's bishop took on g3. Same plan, every game, brainpower saved for the middlegame.

steps.note: The London move. The bishop gets OUTSIDE the pawn chain before White plays e3 — solving the problem the Queen's Gambit bishop on c8 suffers from.
The pawn pyramid begins. c3–d4–e3 will form a granite wedge that Black struggles to attack.
Black strikes at the base... but White's next move makes d4 unshakeable.
The pyramid is complete. Note how many times d4 is now defended.
The knight develops modestly, supporting the e4-break and the e5-outpost for later.
Black offers a trade of the good London bishop. White has a neat answer...
Sidestep! If Black ever captures on g3, White recaptures with the h-pawn and gets a half-open h-file pointing at Black's king. The bishop loses nothing by waiting on g3.
Development complete soon: O-O, and then the two standard plans — plant a knight on e5, or push for e4.
Black prepares to solve their own bishop with ...Bb7 or ...Ba6.

items.title: Countering 1.e4: the Sicilian
items.sub: Fight for a win as Black with the Najdorf setup.
items.intro: 1...c5 is the choice of players who want to WIN as Black. Instead of mirroring White, Black trades a wing pawn for a center pawn and gets an unbalanced game with real winning chances. You are playing Black here — the board is flipped.
items.outro: The Sicilian in one sentence: trade the c-pawn for the d-pawn, then generate queenside counterplay while White attacks on the other wing. It's sharper than 1...e5 — expect richer, messier, more winnable games.

steps.note: The point: c5 controls d4 from the side. White can't build the ideal e4+d4 pawn center without trading — and the trade favors Black structurally.
White prepares d4 anyway.
A quiet, flexible move: controls e5, opens the c8-bishop, and keeps every plan available.
The defining trade: Black gives the c-pawn for White's d-pawn. Black now owns more CENTER pawns (d and e vs White's lone e-pawn) — a small, permanent asset.
Develop with a threat — make White spend a move defending e4.

The Najdorf move, played by Fischer and Kasparov their whole careers. It looks tiny but does three jobs: stops Nb5 and Bb5+ forever, prepares ...e5 without allowing Nb5, and readies ...b5 for queenside expansion.

The thematic strike: the knight is kicked from its central post. The cost is a backward d6-pawn and a hole on d5 — Black accepts this and gets active pieces and space in return. Every opening is a trade-off; strong players just know which trade-offs they've made.
A full Najdorf position. Black's plans: ...Be6, ...Nbd7, ...b5 and queenside play, while keeping an eye on White's f4 or Bg5 tries.

items.title: Countering 1.e4: the Caro-Kann
items.sub: The solid choice — a fortress that still fights.
items.intro: If the Sicilian feels too sharp, the Caro-Kann (1...c6) is the pro-level "solid" answer to 1.e4. Its whole philosophy: build ...d5 with support, and — unlike the French — develop the light-squared bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain before closing it in. You are Black; board flipped.
items.outro: Caro-Kann in one sentence: solve the bishop first, then build the indestructible e6+c6 wall. Your middlegame plan is nearly always the ...c5 pawn break. Quiet, sound, and very hard to beat.

steps.note: A preparation move: next comes ...d5, challenging e4 with full pawn support.
White takes the big center while allowed.
The challenge. White must now defend, push, or trade e4.
Defending e4 with development.
Black trades in the classical main line — happy to let White's knight recapture, because the knight can then be harassed.

THE Caro-Kann move. The problem bishop develops actively with tempo — attacking the knight — before Black plays ...e6 and locks the pawn chain. Compare the French Defense, where this bishop often rots on c8 for 30 moves.
The knight returns the favor, hitting the bishop.
The bishop slides to safety, still on its best diagonal.
White tries to trap or annoy the bishop with the h-pawn's advance. Black must respond precisely — and the response is worth memorizing.
Making an escape hatch on h7 for the bishop. Now h5 can be met by ...Bh7 forever.
Flexible development: this knight supports a later ...Ngf6 (so that a trade on f6 can be answered with the knight, not wrecking the pawns).
Exactly as prepared. The bishop is safe and STILL on the b1–h7 diagonal.
White offers the trade to neutralize it.
Only NOW does Black play ...e6 — with the bishop already traded, closing the chain costs nothing. The rest writes itself: ...Ngf6, ...Be7, ...O-O, then the ...c5 break.

items.title: Traps you must know
items.sub: Légal's mate and the Scholar's mate defense.
items.intro: You don't study traps to play cheap chess — you study them so they never happen to YOU, and to learn the deeper lessons they encode. Two classics: a false pin, and the early queen raid.
items.outro: Two permanent lessons: (1) pins against the queen can be broken by force — always calculate the "impossible" capture; (2) meet early queen attacks with developing moves that defend, and collect free tempi by attacking the queen. Never panic, never mirror.

steps.note: Trap one: Légal's mate. Watch what happens to a player who trusts a pin too much.
The passive Philidor setup — playable, but Black must stay alert.
Black "pins" the knight to the queen. But read carefully: this is a pin to the QUEEN, not the king. The knight may still legally move — it's only a question of arithmetic.
White develops... and quietly sets the trap.
A wasted move that ignores development. Black believes the f3-knight is glued in place. Now count along with White...
The knight moves anyway! If Black just recaptures with 5...dxe5, White plays 6.Qxg4 and has won a clean pawn. But the "free" queen is poisoned...
Greed. Black takes the queen — and gets mated by minor pieces in two moves.
Forced.
Checkmate. Three minor pieces beat a queen that never left home. The lesson: a pin against the queen is a suggestion, not a law. Always check what happens if the "pinned" piece moves anyway.
Trap two: the Scholar's Mate — the 4-move mate every beginner has suffered. Here is the correct, permanent antidote.
The queen raid: threatening both Qxe5 and the mate on f7. Objectively a bad move — but only if you know the recipe. Rule: parry the threat WITH a developing move.
Defends e5 and develops. Never weaken yourself with moves like ...g6 here (which drops e5), and never mirror with ...Qh4?.
The mate threat on f7 is renewed — two attackers now.
NOW ...g6 is right: it hits the queen, gaining a whole tempo. The queen must move again — her third move while Black develops.
Stubborn: threatening mate on f7 a third time, down the f-file.
Development blocks the file and ends the circus. Count the score: White moved the queen three times; Black developed two knights and gained the g6 space. Black is already better.

items.title: Drill: punish 2...f6?
items.sub: Your opponent weakened the king. Make them regret it.
items.intro: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 your opponent played 2...f6? — defending e5 while opening the worst diagonal on the board toward their own king. This mistake has a forced punishment known since 1512. Find it: it begins with a sacrifice.
items.outro: A full rook up on move six. Remember both halves: never play ...f6 in front of your king in the opening — and when your opponent does, look hard at Nxe5 followed by Qh5+. The pattern recurs at every level below master.
items.hint: The f6-pawn "defends" e5 — but what happens to Black's king if you give up the knight and bring the queen to h5?

line.note: Correct — a real sacrifice. If Black declines with 3...Qe7, you retreat 4.Nf3 and simply enjoy a free pawn. Here Black grabs the knight...
Now the punishment.

The point of the sacrifice: the check rakes the weakened diagonal. Black's best try is 4...Ke7, which loses the king's right to live quietly; 4...g6 loses material at once — and that's what happens here.
Blocking — but now both e5 and h8 hang on the same diagonal-and-rank fork...
Check AND attacking the rook in the corner. A queen fork — Black can only block.
Forced. One more move finishes the job.

title: Tactics & Techniques
blurb: The seven patterns that decide most games under 2000.

items.title: The back-rank mate
items.sub: The most common mate in amateur chess.
items.intro: Both sides castled long ago; both kings sit behind an unmoved wall of pawns. Your opponent just grabbed your h-pawn with the rook — a pawn they will never get to enjoy. Their king's own pawn shelter has become a prison. One move ends the game.
items.outro: Mate: the pawns on f7, g7, h7 seal every exit. Two habits to build: (1) whenever the enemy back rank is bare, look for a rook or queen landing; (2) in YOUR OWN games, spend one move on h3/h6 ("luft") before your back rank gets thin. Half of all club-level blunders trace back to this pattern.
items.hint: Black's rook wandered away from the 8th rank. Who controls the d-file?

items.title: The knight fork
items.sub: One piece, two targets, no defense.
items.intro: A fork attacks two things at once — the opponent can only save one. Knights are the fork specialists because their attack can't be blocked and they hit squares no other piece is watching. Here your centralized knight has a famous jump available. Check every square it can reach: which one touches TWO royals?
items.outro: Queen for a knight — a winning material edge. Training habit: on EVERY move, glance at your knights and ask "what does this knight hit two moves from now?" And keep your own king and queen off squares a single knight-jump apart.
items.hint: A check that also attacks the queen. Look at the e7 square.

line.note: The royal fork: check to the king on g8, attack on the queen on c8. Black must deal with the check.
Now collect.
The queen falls. Black gets the knight back...

items.title: The pin — then pile on
items.sub: A pinned piece isn't just stuck. It's a target.
items.intro: Your rook on e1 pins Black's knight to the king — an ABSOLUTE pin, so the knight legally cannot move. But a pin by itself wins nothing. The rule of pins: attack the pinned piece AGAIN, with something cheap. What's the cheapest attacker you have?
items.outro: A whole piece for nothing. The complete pin recipe: (1) spot pieces lined up with their king or queen, (2) pin with a bishop or rook, (3) pile on with pawns. And remember from the Traps lesson: only pins against the KING are absolute — pins against the queen can be broken by a countertactic.
items.hint: Pawns are the perfect executioners of pinned pieces. Which pawn can step forward and attack e5?

line.note: The knight is attacked by a pawn and cannot run — moving it is illegal while the king sits on e8. Black's only hope is to unpin...
The king steps off the file, unpinning the knight — but it's White's turn.

items.title: The skewer
items.sub: A pin in reverse: the big piece is forced to step aside.
items.intro: A skewer is a pin flipped around: the MORE valuable piece stands in front and must move, exposing what's behind. Black's king has wandered to d7 — and behind it, on the same diagonal, sits the queen. Your bishop is one move from the right line.
items.outro: Queen for a bishop. Skewers love long open lines and exposed kings — which is why they decide so many endgames (you'll meet one deciding a pawn race in the Endgames chapter). Habit: whenever the enemy king and a big piece share a line, look for the check that exploits it.
items.goal: Win the queen for a bishop (2 moves).
items.hint: Find the diagonal that passes through both d7 and c8.

line.note: Check. The king must move — nothing can block (trace the line: g4, f5, e6 — no Black piece can reach any of them).
And now the piece behind is bare.

items.title: The discovered attack
items.sub: One move, two attacks from two different pieces.
items.intro: The most violent tactic in chess: move one piece, and the piece BEHIND it attacks something too. Your knight on d5 stands in front of your rook on d1 — and Black's queen is on d7, on that very file. The knight can go anywhere... so send it somewhere that creates a SECOND threat. The deadliest version gives check.
items.outro: Queen for a knight. Discovered attacks are why you must notice every time TWO pieces (one yours, one theirs, or a battery of yours) share a line with something in between. The in-between piece becomes a launched missile — it can move anywhere, even to "impossible" squares, because the discovered threat pays for it.
items.hint: Which knight move gives check to the king on g8? The rook handles the queen by itself.

line.note: Double trouble: the knight checks the king while the rook's attack on the queen is unveiled. Black cannot answer both — the check comes first by law. (1...Kh8 loses even faster: 2.Nxd7 takes the queen with the knight.)
The knight is captured — but it already did its job.

items.title: Deflection: the overworked defender
items.sub: The prettiest sacrifice in club chess.
items.intro: Look at Black's queen on d8: she is the ONLY piece guarding the e8 entry square — the back-rank mate you already know. A defender with a job can be dragged away from it, if you're willing to pay. Your queen and rook both point at e8. Count what happens if you simply crash in.
items.outro: The deflection formula: (1) find the enemy piece holding everything together, (2) ask "what would I play if it vanished?", (3) if that answer is strong enough — mate, or winning material — you can afford to sacrifice to drag it away. Every "brilliant" queen sac you've seen online is this formula wearing makeup.
items.hint: Your queen can reach e8 along the a4–e8 diagonal. Yes, Black can capture her. Look one move deeper.

line.note: A full queen sacrifice — the point is that Black's queen is FORCED to take (the rook on b8 is blocked by her own queen, and the king can't reach e8), and taking drags her off the back rank...
The defender has been deflected. Now the mate you know.

items.title: The smothered mate
items.sub: Philidor's Legacy — the most beautiful forced sequence in chess.
items.intro: A king "smothered" by his own pieces can be mated by a lone knight. The full mechanism — check, double check, queen sacrifice, mate — is 500 years old and still wins games every day. Watch each gear turn.
items.outro: Memorize the gear sequence: Q-check to drive the king to the corner → N-check → N double-check (the only way to force the king BACK) → Q-sac on g8 → N-mate on f7. When you have a queen on the a2–g8 diagonal and a knight near g5, this is never far away.

steps.note: The queen takes the diagonal to g8 with check. (If Black blocks with 1...Rf7?, then 2.Nxf7 wins material anyway.) The king has one dignified square...
Into the corner. Now the knight begins its dance.
Check. Note Black could bail out here with 2...Rxf7 3.Qxf7 — losing an exchange but surviving. Greedy defenders retreat the king instead...
DOUBLE check — knight and queen hit g8 simultaneously. Against double check there is no capture and no block: the king MUST move. And with the rook on f8, the only square is back to the corner.
Now the move that makes this sequence famous.
The queen sacrifices herself on a square defended by rook AND king. But the king can't take (the knight on h6 guards g8!) — so the rook must.
And now the king is buried alive: rook on g8, pawns on g7 and h7 — his own army seals the tomb.
Smothered mate. The knight — the only piece whose attack passes through walls — delivers the end alone.

title: Thinking Ahead
blurb: The calculation habits that separate improving players from stuck ones.

items.title: Checks, Captures, Threats
items.sub: The scan that catches blunders before you make them.
items.intro: Strong players don't calculate everything — they calculate the FORCING moves: every Check, every Capture, every Threat (CCT), for both sides, before anything else. Forcing moves have forced answers, so they're the only lines you can calculate reliably. Watch CCT expose a "blunder" that isn't one.
items.outro: The routine to burn in: before EVERY move, list the opponent's checks, captures and threats against you; after choosing your candidate move, list THEIR checks, captures and threats in the new position. Thirty seconds of CCT prevents 90% of amateur blunders. This is the single highest-value habit in this entire course.

steps.note: A normal position. Now Black plays something that looks like a one-move blunder...
The knight takes a defended pawn?! A lazy scan says "Black just loses a piece to Nxe4." But CCT demands you follow the forcing moves to the END of the line. Watch.
White grabs the piece. Now find Black's forcing moves: no good checks... but there is a terrible THREAT-move.
The fork trick: one pawn attacks BOTH the knight and the bishop. White must lose one of them back. This is why you calculate to the end of the forcing sequence before judging a capture.
White saves the bishop (best), conceding the knight.

Count the final ledger: knight for knight, pawn for pawn. Dead equal. Black's "blunder" was a clean equalizing trick — visible only to players who follow checks, captures and threats all the way down.

items.title: Reading the attack signals
items.sub: How strong players "see" attacks before they exist.
items.intro: Attacks don't appear from nowhere — the position broadcasts signals first. Learn the three loudest ones and you'll spot attacking chances (and dangers to yourself) a full phase earlier. Three diagrams, three signals.
items.outro: Your pre-move scan, upgraded: (1) CCT, (2) any king on an open line? (3) any loose pieces, mine or theirs? (4) how's my back rank? Four questions, ten seconds, hundreds of rating points.

steps.note: SIGNAL 1 — King in the center + open file. Black hasn't castled and the e-file is fully open: White's rook stares straight through to e8. Every White move now comes with a tactical bonus. When you see an uncastled king on an open file — yours or theirs — the alarm should be deafening. (Black here must castle IMMEDIATELY.)

SIGNAL 2 — Loose pieces. Black's bishop on a6 and knight on h5 are both UNDEFENDED. "Loose Pieces Drop Off": here White plays Qa5!, forking both along the rank and file — check it: the queen attacks a6 and h5 simultaneously, and no Black piece can guard both. Before every move, scan for undefended units on both sides. Tactics are 80% loose pieces.

SIGNAL 3 — The airless back rank. Both kings here have zero escape squares — a mutual mate-in-one waiting for whoever wins the d-file argument. The moment queens and rooks remain and your pawn shield is unmoved, budget one move for h3 (or ...h6). Cheap insurance against the most common mate in chess.

items.title: Drill: see their threat first
items.sub: Half of thinking ahead is thinking about THEIR next move.
items.intro: Your opponent just swung the queen to h5, joining the knight on g4. Run the CCT scan for BLACK before you touch anything: what are they threatening to play next move? Once you see it, the defensive requirement becomes precise — most natural moves here lose on the spot.
items.outro: The knight retreats and the attack is over — you keep your extra material and the better game. The lesson: every turn has TWO halves — "what do I want?" and "what do they want?" Players who skip the second half donate hundreds of games to mates they never saw coming.
items.goal: Find the only move that survives.
items.hint: Black threatens ...Qxh2# — the queen protected by the g4-knight, your king with no escape. You can't defend h2 enough times... so evict the supporting attacker.

line.note: The only real defense: the pawn attacks the knight AND opens breathing room. The mate needed the knight's protection — remove the accomplice, and the threat dies. (1...Nxf2? loses a piece to 2.Rxf2, and 1...Qxh3?? 2.gxh3 loses the queen.)

items.title: Drill: calculate three moves deep
items.sub: A queen sacrifice you can verify before you play it.
items.intro: This is the graduation exercise. There is a forced mate in three here, and it costs your queen. Don't guess — CALCULATE: start with your checks (you have two pieces that can give one), follow each forced reply, and only play the first move once you've seen the final position in your head. The pattern is called Anastasia's mate.
items.outro: Anastasia's mate: the e7-knight covers g8 and g6, the rook owns the h-file, the king has nowhere left. You just calculated a three-move combination with a queen sacrifice — the exact skill, at the exact depth, that wins games at club level. The formula never changes: forcing moves only, follow every forced reply, verify the end before you begin.
items.hint: Start with the knight check on e7 — it takes away the g8 and... which other square? Then ask what your queen's most violent follow-up is on the h-file.

line.note: The knight seals g8 AND g6 — remember that; it matters two moves from now. (If 1...Qxe7 instead, 2.Rxe7 simply wins the queen.)
Now the move you had to see in advance...
The queen gives herself up to drag the king onto the open h-file. Capture is forced — and your rook is one quiet step from h1.
Finish it.

title: Endgames
blurb: Where casual players give away half their results — and where you stop.

items.title: King & pawn: the opposition
items.sub: The single most important idea in all endgames.
items.intro: Two kings facing each other with one square between them are "in opposition" — and whoever does NOT have to move wins the standoff, because the other king must step aside. Most king-and-pawn endgames are decided purely by this. Watch White convert an extra pawn with it.
items.outro: Three rules to keep forever: (1) king IN FRONT of its pawn wins (except rook-pawns); (2) grab the opposition — force the enemy king to move first; (3) use spare pawn moves to pass the "hot potato" back. Master these and you'll convert endgames your opponents assume are drawn.

steps.note: The kings were face to face with White to move — normally bad! But the pawn gives White a priceless resource: spare moves. White steps DIAGONALLY sideways, keeping control of the key squares d7 and e7. (1.e6? at once would let Black hold with precise play.)
Black keeps blocking the path. Now the pawn advances — with the king already escorting AHEAD of it. King in front of pawn = win. Pawn in front of king = usually a draw.
Black takes the opposition... but White has a spare pawn move — the tempo-breaker.

The pawn itself steals the opposition back! Black's king must now leave the promotion square. (Careful: if this pawn advance came WITH CHECK, it would only draw — a detail that decides thousands of games.)
The king seizes e8's guardianship. Nothing can stop promotion now.
A new queen. From here, the K+Q mate you'll learn next door finishes in a few moves.

THE DRAWN VERSION, for contrast: here the pawn is AHEAD of its king. With correct defense — Black's king simply stays in front of the pawn and takes the opposition at every chance — this is a dead draw. Same material, opposite result. The king's position, not the pawn count, decides these endings.

items.title: Drill: only one move wins
items.sub: Apply the opposition yourself.
items.intro: White is a clean pawn up — but two of the three sensible moves here only DRAW. Remember the rules: king ahead of the pawn, and take the opposition (kings facing, one gap, opponent to move). One move does both.
items.outro: Correct — the king strides in front of its pawn AND seizes the opposition: Black must give way, and White's king walks to f6 or d6 escorting the pawn home. Both 1.e5? (pawn ahead of king — Black blockades with ...Ke6-ish holds) and 1.Kc5? (...Kd7 keeps the door shut) are theoretical draws. One tempo, one square — the whole game.
items.hint: Pushing the pawn lets Black's king plant itself in front and hold forever. Where must YOUR king go instead?

items.title: Drill: the rule of the square
items.sub: Know in one glance whether a pawn outruns a king.
items.intro: Can Black's king catch your runner? Don't count moves one by one — draw the SQUARE: from the pawn (b5) to its promotion rank (b8), then sideways the same distance (b8–e8, e8–e5). If the defending king can step INTO that square on its move, it catches the pawn. Black's king on f7 is outside it. So?
items.outro: Promoted, and the new queen is safely out of the king's reach. The square rule turns a 6-move calculation into a one-glance check — use it every time a passed pawn starts running, on either side of the board. (Extra tempo warning: if the pawn were still on its home square, remember its double-step when drawing the square.)
items.hint: The king is outside the square — every tempo spent on anything but pushing is a tempo wasted.

line.note: Run! (1.Kf3?? would let the king step into the square with 1...Ke7 and hold the draw.)
Chasing — one step too late.

items.title: Mating with king & queen
items.sub: The box method — and the stalemate trap that ruins it.
items.intro: You promoted; now finish cleanly. The reliable technique: use the queen ALONE to shrink a box around the enemy king — keeping her a knight's-move away so there are no checks and no accidents — then bring your king over for the final two-piece mate. No checks until the end!
items.outro: The routine: (1) queen to a knight's-move away, no checks; (2) mirror the king's steps, shrinking the box; (3) STOP at the edge; (4) walk your king up; (5) mate on the edge. Practice until it's 15 seconds of autopilot — and never stalemate anyone again.

steps.note: A knight's-move from the enemy king. Look at the cage: the queen's lines fence the king into the small region up-and-left. No check was given — checks just chase the king around; the CAGE is what traps him.
The king shuffles. The queen mirrors — always a knight's-move away.
The box shrinks.
Smaller.
Smaller still — the king is nearly on the edge.
The king is on the edge. Boxing phase complete — and here the technique CHANGES.

STOP boxing once the king reaches the edge — one more squeeze risks stalemate. Instead the queen holds the cage while your own king marches over (we've fast-forwarded that walk). Now, with your king adjacent-ish, one move ends it.
Mate: the queen covers the back rank, your king covers every square in front. The standard finish.

THE TRAP that has ruined a million winning games: Black to move here has NO legal move and is NOT in check — STALEMATE, instant draw. This is why the box method forbids putting the queen a mere king-step away from a cornered king unless it's mate. When the enemy king is on the edge, pause and count his legal moves before every queen move.

items.title: Rook endgame I: the Lucena
items.sub: "Building a bridge" — the most famous winning method in chess.
items.intro: Rook endgames are the most common endgames in chess, and this is their most important position. White's pawn sits one step from promotion, but White's own king blocks it and Black's rook stands ready to check forever. The winning method — the "bridge" — is 500 years old. If you learn ONE rook endgame position in your life, it's this one.
items.outro: The Lucena recipe: rook to the 4th rank FIRST, push the enemy king away with a check, walk your king out, zig-zag down through the checks, then block with the rook-bridge. If your rook-and-pawn endgame is winning, this is HOW it's winning — steer for it deliberately.

steps.note: The mysterious key move: the rook goes to the FOURTH rank for reasons that only become clear five moves later. (Why not just walk the king out? Try it mentally: 1.Kc8?? is illegal here, and after any king exit Black checks from behind forever unless the bridge is ready.)
Black can only wait and prepare checks.
First, shoulder the Black king farther away from the pawn.
Now the White king can finally step out.
Threatening to promote next move. Black's only weapon: the checking machine.
Check!
Check again — is this a draw by endless checks? Watch the king's path carefully.
The king zig-zags DOWN the board, one file at a time...
...luring the rook's checks closer to the 4th rank...
One last check. And now you see why the rook went to c4 on move one.
THE BRIDGE. The rook interposes, protected by its own king, and the checks are over forever. Black is helpless.
The pawn promotes. Game over.

items.title: Rook endgame II: the Philidor draw
items.sub: A pawn down in a rook endgame? Hold the draw on autopilot.
items.intro: The flip side of the Lucena: you're DEFENDING a rook endgame a pawn down. Played correctly, this position is a bulletproof draw — the method is two rules and zero calculation. You're Black (board flipped). Rule one: patrol your third rank.
items.outro: The Philidor autopilot: (1) rook patrols your third rank so the enemy king can't cross; (2) the moment the pawn reaches that rank, rook to the far end of the board and check from behind forever. Two rules, zero losses. This single technique will save you dozens of half-points.

steps.note: The rook patrols the 6th rank (YOUR third rank) like a tripwire: White's king can never cross to d6 or f6 to escort the pawn. As long as the pawn stays back, you just shuffle along this rank. Do not check "for activity." Do not grab pawns. Patrol.
White's only real try: advancing the pawn to make way for the king. But the pawn's advance is exactly your cue — RULE TWO...

The instant the pawn steps onto your patrol rank, the rook drops ALL the way back — because now the White king has no shelter from behind-checks: the pawn can no longer shield him on e5 (he needs that square himself).
White threatens to force the pawn through with king support. Now the checking machine starts — with a clear conscience, because it can never run out.
Check.
Not even a check — just re-aiming at the pawn. The king can't hide in front of it (it needs to defend it) and can't make progress: if he steps away from the pawn, you take it.
White tries the other side...
...and the checks resume. There is no shelter anywhere on the board.
Repetition. White has nothing better — the game is a dead draw.

items.title: Drill: win the pawn race
items.sub: Both sides promoted. One tactic decides.
items.intro: The pawn race ended in a photo finish: you promoted first, Black promoted right after — while their king escorted the pawn home. Material is even... for one more move. Look at Black's king and brand-new queen: what LINE do they share? You learned this pattern in the Tactics chapter.
items.outro: A full queen, and the K+Q mate you've already mastered finishes the game. This skewer is THE standard finish to pawn races — which teaches a deeper habit: when racing, glance at where both kings will stand at the finish line. Promoting FIRST matters less than promoting SAFELY; sometimes the winning race move is a king step that dodges this exact skewer.
items.hint: King on d1, queen on a1 — both on the first rank. Your queen wants that rank, with check.

line.note: The skewer. The king must step off the rank — no blocks exist, and every escape square abandons the queen.
